authority: Candidate only. Importing creates candidate claims authored by the person who imports them; a different signed-in person must verify each one, and nothing is released or activated by the import.

claims.title: Bounded retry for transient faults
claims.statement: Bounded retry for transient faults: Classify the failure, bound attempts and elapsed time, and space retries according to the dependency and caller budget. Preserve an exhausted outcome instead of retrying indefinitely.
conditions: This candidate addresses transient rather than terminal faults.
A repeated operation needs an evidenced safe outcome, not merely an assumed lost request.
Retry duration and load must fit the actual caller requirements.
limitations: Permanent validation or business-logic errors and persistent overload need another treatment; retry does not replace capacity work.
Additional attempts can increase latency and pressure on an already busy dependency; nested retry policies can amplify both.

claims.title: Unknown outcome after a lost response
claims.statement: Unknown outcome after a lost response: Represent the outcome as unresolved until an authoritative status or repeat-safe operation protocol establishes what happened; do not convert transport failure into known business failure.
conditions: The concern is consequential repeat execution, not a read-only request.
This investigation targets an unresolved first outcome.
limitations: This does not invent a status endpoint, safe repeat guarantee or automatic compensating action.
Tracking operation identity and status adds contract, retention and reconciliation obligations; the authoritative owner must be established.

claims.title: Retry-storm investigation and containment
claims.statement: Retry-storm investigation and containment: Investigate retry frequency and duration; bound attempts, introduce appropriate spacing, respect applicable server retry guidance, and stop when the caller no longer has a useful request.
conditions: This is a grounded diagnostic, not a defect inferred from the mere presence of retry code.
The observed attempts must be connected to the affected dependency/recovery concern.
limitations: An isolated failure or an invalid request alone does not demonstrate a retry storm.
Reducing attempts may expose failures sooner to callers; the desired degradation and recovery behaviour must be designed.

claims.title: Circuit breaker with controlled recovery probes
claims.statement: Circuit breaker with controlled recovery probes: Observe scoped failures, open to reject calls, and allow limited half-open probes before restoring normal calls. Retry policy must respect the open state.
conditions: A prolonged or repeated dependency fault motivates this treatment.
The caller needs an explicit response when calls are rejected.
limitations: A breaker does not fix the failed service or establish the business outcome of a request already sent.
An open breaker deliberately rejects work; thresholds, reset conditions and recovery probes require workload-specific evaluation.

claims.title: Partition scarce resources to contain failure
claims.statement: Partition scarce resources to contain failure: Partition the relevant service capacity, connection pools or resources so one workload cannot consume the entire shared pool.
conditions: The candidate needs a recorded shared-resource pressure.
Isolation must refer to a named resource/boundary rather than just drawing separate boxes.
limitations: Reject unnecessary partitions when their complexity or less efficient resource use is not justified.
Reserved capacity and more partitions can reduce utilisation efficiency and increase operating complexity.

claims.title: Dead-letter isolation and controlled recovery
claims.statement: Dead-letter isolation and controlled recovery: After an explicit failure threshold, isolate the message with its failure context for analysis and controlled resubmission rather than immediate endless cycling.
conditions: A recorded non-progressing message or persistent processing failure motivates isolation.
Stored failed work needs an accountable investigation/recovery path.
limitations: Moving a message does not prove it was successfully processed or that resubmitting it is safe.
Failure storage needs monitoring, retention and controlled replay. In the captured Camel example, a failure sending to the dead-letter endpoint has its own configurable propagation behaviour.

claims.title: Asynchronous request acceptance and status contract
claims.statement: Asynchronous request acceptance and status contract: Separate admission from completion: acknowledge accepted processing, return a status location and expose progress/completion through a defined status resource.
conditions: The pattern addresses deferred completion.
The client must support the agreed status observation protocol.
A status resource needs an actual authoritative owner and lifecycle.
limitations: An accepted response is not completed work; the pattern does not fabricate a status endpoint for an external system that lacks one.
Polling, retention, cancellation and resubmission introduce contracts and operating load; a lost initial response can still repeat work without suitable identity handling.

claims.title: Queue-based load leveling with bounded downstream pressure
claims.statement: Queue-based load leveling with bounded downstream pressure: Buffer admitted work and let consumers process it at a controlled rate, with explicit durability, capacity, retention and overload policy.
conditions: Intake and processing must be separable.
A recorded burst pressure motivates load leveling.
Unbounded consumer autoscaling can move overload downstream.
limitations: A queue cannot solve a sustained producer rate above sustainable service rate without capacity, admission or work-shedding changes.
Buffering adds latency and storage limits; durability, duplicate processing and ordering must be examined separately.

claims.title: Competing consumers for independently processable work
claims.statement: Competing consumers for independently processable work: Let multiple worker instances receive work from an appropriate queue, while explicitly handling duplicates, poison messages, completion and ordering.
conditions: The captured source limits this treatment where tasks are highly dependent.
Strict synchronous completion may rule out this pattern.
Strict sequence requirements need an explicit ordering mechanism or another design.
limitations: Do not infer ordering correctness from idempotence alone. Independent handling and any required ordering mechanism need their own evidence.
More workers add downstream contention; duplicate delivery and poison-message policies remain necessary.

claims.title: Publish-subscribe with explicit subscriber obligations
claims.statement: Publish-subscribe with explicit subscriber obligations: Publish a defined message to a channel and distribute it to interested subscriptions; declare subscription, security, ordering and reply semantics separately.
conditions: The treatment is fan-out to interested subscribers, not task competition.
Subscribers receive through a separate asynchronous mechanism.
limitations: A pub/sub label alone does not guarantee offline delivery, ordering or durable replay; those depend on the chosen infrastructure and subscription configuration.
Topic granularity, per-topic permissions, message compatibility and reverse status paths create additional responsibilities.

claims.title: Business-specific compensating transactions
claims.statement: Business-specific compensating transactions: Record completed steps and their business-specific corrective actions, account for concurrent work, and keep compensation resumable with safe repeated steps.
conditions: This treatment addresses work that cannot simply use one existing atomic transaction.
Undo behaviour must be meaningful under the domain rules.
Recovery must retain the information needed to resume failed compensation.
limitations: Irreversible steps and legally/business-significant effects cannot be made reversible by labelling them compensation.
Compensation can itself fail, may not restore the exact original state, and may need human intervention; transient retry may be simpler for recoverable faults.

claims.title: Spring Modulith transactional publication registry
claims.statement: Spring Modulith transactional publication registry: The captured Spring Modulith implementation records one log entry per transactional listener within the business transaction, marks successful completion, and retains incomplete work for explicit resubmission policies.
conditions: The documented lifecycle is implementation-specific.
The registry hooks into the documented transactional-listener contract.
The publication log must participate in the original transaction.
limitations: Do not assume automatic restart replay or stale-work monitoring is enabled; these depend on the captured configuration and version.
Publication records require retention/cleanup and safe repeat handling. Completed-record accumulation can increase storage and slow registry interactions.

claims.title: Spring Modulith event externalisation and ordering
claims.statement: Spring Modulith event externalisation and ordering: Select events, deliberately map external payloads and route them through the documented broker-specific publication integration. Review resubmission and externalisation serialisation where order matters.
conditions: These details apply to the captured Spring Modulith event implementation.
Externalisation needs an actual external consumer or contract.
Internal event type names are not automatically suitable public contracts.
limitations: Do not presume publication order survives asynchronous resubmission; serialization is a configurable implementation choice, not a global guarantee.
Serializing external publication can constrain concurrency, while parallel publication can reorder events. External payload and routing become separate versioned obligations.

claims.title: Explicit module APIs and implementation boundaries
claims.statement: Explicit module APIs and implementation boundaries: For the captured Spring Modulith packaging model, distinguish provided API, internal components and required APIs. Check module openness and named interfaces before treating an access as forbidden.
conditions: The package/API mapping belongs to the captured framework model.
A boundary must identify actual packages and declared interfaces.
limitations: An explicitly open module has different verification semantics and may be an intentional migration step, not an automatically prohibited design.
Encapsulation supports local change but demands deliberate API design and migration work for existing cross-module dependencies.

claims.title: Verify module dependency cycles and API access
claims.statement: Verify module dependency cycles and API access: The captured verifier checks the module dependency graph, API-only access with documented open-module exceptions, and optional allowed-dependency declarations.
conditions: The recipe names the captured framework verifier, not all programming languages.
Verification needs the actual implementation graph, not a hand-drawn model.
limitations: No executed result is supplied here; a verification recipe does not certify the users application, runtime behaviour or business correctness.
Policy configuration and migration exceptions affect which dependencies are admitted; ignored violations must not silently become a clean result.

claims.title: Opt-in module dependency allowlists
claims.statement: Opt-in module dependency allowlists: Declare allowed dependencies explicitly in the captured module metadata, and verify the code against that policy; absence of the optional declaration must not be presented as an enforced allowlist.
conditions: The annotation and validation contract are framework-specific.
The additional restriction needs an actual design requirement.
The source describes an opt-in rule; no declaration means no evidence of this enforcement.
limitations: A general public API boundary does not prove this optional allowed-dependency policy has been configured.
A restrictive allowlist adds intentional change control; required integrations must be reviewed rather than silently bypassing the declaration.
